    #Part (b)

    Note that the differential equation is 2x¨+2x˙+x=0,
    and the initial conditions are     x(0)=0 and x′(0)=4.

    Laplace transform of x¨,

    L{x¨}=s2X(s)−sx(0)−x′(0)

    L{x¨}=s2X(s)−4

    Laplace transform of x˙,

    L{x˙}=sX(s)−x(0)

    L{x˙}=sX(s)

    Performing Laplace transform,

    2x¨+2x˙+x=0

    2(s2X−4)+2(sX)+X=0

    2s2X−8+2sX+X=0

    (2s2+2s+1)X=8

    X=2s2+2s+18​

    X=s2+s+0.54​

    Completing the square for the denominator,

    X=(s+0.5)2+0.524​

    X=0.54​⋅(s+0.5)2+0.520.5​

    Performing inverse Laplace transform,

    x(t)=8e−21​tsin21​t

    #Question 2

    Step 1

    Swap the positions of the 2nd and 3rd summing junctions.

    Step 2

    Determine transfer function of G2​ and H2​ closed loop.

    T.F.=1+G2​H2​G2​​

    Step 3

    Shift take off point of H1​ to after G3​.

    Step 4

    Determine transfer function of 1+G2​H2​G2​G3​​ and H3​.

    Denominator of transfer function,

    1+1+G2​H2​G2​G3​​⋅H3​

    =1+1+G2​H2​G2​G3​H3​​

    =1+G2​H2​1+G2​H2​+G2​G3​H3​​

    Transfer function,

    T.F.=1+G2​H2​G2​G3​​⋅1+G2​H2​+G2​G3​H3​1+G2​H2​​

    T.F.=1+G2​H2​+G2​G3​H3​G2​G3​​

    Step 5

    Determine transfer function of 1+G2​H2​+G2​G3​H3​G1​G2​G3​​ and G3​H1​​.

    Denominator of transfer function,

    1+1+G2​H2​+G2​G3​H3​G1​G2​G3​​⋅G3​H1​​

    =1+1+G2​H2​+G2​G3​H3​G1​G2​H1​​

    =1+G2​G3​+G2​G3​H3​1+G2​H2​+G1​G2​H1​+G2​G3​H3​​

    Transfer function,

    T.F.=1+G2​G3​+G2​G3​H3​G1​G2​G3​​⋅1+G2​H2​+G1​G2​H1​+G2​G3​H3​1+G2​G3​+G2​G3​H3​​

    T.F.=1+G2​H2​+G1​G2​H1​+G2​G3​H3​G1​G2​G3​​

    #Question 3

    #Part (a)

    Assume u>x. Thus, the spring and damper are in compression.

    Using Newton’s 2nd law on the mass,

    mx¨=c(u˙−x˙)+k(u−x)

    mx¨=cu˙−cx˙+ku−kx

    mx¨+cx˙+kx=cu˙+ku

    Performing Laplace transform,

    m⋅s2X(s)+c⋅sX(s)+kX(s)=c⋅sU(s)+kU(s)

    (ms2+cs+k)⋅X(s)=(cs+k)⋅U(s)

    U(s)X(s)​=ms2+cs+kcs+k​

    #Part (b)

    Unit step input where U(s)=s1​,

    X(s)=s1​⋅ms2+cs+kcs+k​

    X(s)=s(ms2+cs+k)cs+k​

    Using final value theorem,

    t→∞lim​ f(t)=s→0lim​ sF(s)

    xss​=s→0lim​ s⋅s(ms2+cs+k)cs+k​

    xss​=s→0lim​ ms2+cs+kcs+k​

    xss​=1

    #Part (c)

    Using initial value theorem,

    t→0lim​ f(t)=s→∞lim​ sF(s)

    x(0)=s→∞lim​ s⋅s(ms2+cs+k)cs+k​

    x(0)=s→∞lim​ ms2+cs+kcs+k​

    x(0)=0

    #Part (d)

    Using initial value theorem,

    t→0lim​ f′(t)=s→∞lim​ sL{f′(t)}

    x′(0)=s→∞lim​ sL{x′(t)}

    x′(0)=s→∞lim​ s⋅ms2+2s+kcs+k​

    x′(0)=s→∞lim​ ms2+2s+kcs2+ks​

    x′(0)=s→∞lim​ 2ms+22cs+k​

    x′(0)=s→∞lim​ 2m2c​

    x′(0)=mc​

    Laplace transform of first derivative,

    L{x′(t)}=sX(s)−x(0)

    L{x′(t)}=s⋅s(ms2+2s+k)cs+k​

    L{x′(t)}=ms2+2s+kcs+k​

    #Question 3

    Assume y>z>x. Thus, the springs and damper are in compression.

    Using Newton’s 2nd law on m1​,

    m1​z¨=kt​(y−z)−kb​(z−x)−c(z˙−x˙)

    m1​z¨=(−kt​−kb​)z−cz˙+kt​y+kb​x+cx˙

    m1​z¨+cz˙+(kt​+kb​)z=kt​y+kb​x+cx˙

    Performing Laplace transform,

    m1​⋅s2Z(s)+c⋅sZ(s)+(kt​+kb​)⋅Z(s)=kt​Y(s)+kb​X(s)+c⋅sX(s)

    (m1​s2+cs+kt​+kb​)⋅Z(s)=kt​Y(s)+kb​X(s)+c⋅sX(s)

    (m1​s2+cs+kt​+kb​)⋅Z(s)=kt​Y(s)+(cs+kb​)⋅X(s)

    Using Newton’s 2nd law on m2​,

    m2​x¨=kb​(z−x)+c(z˙−x˙)

    m2​x¨=kb​z−kb​x+cz˙−cx˙

    m2​x¨+cx˙+kb​x=cz˙+kb​z

    Performing Laplace transform,

    m2​⋅s2X(s)+c⋅sX(s)+kb​X(s)=c⋅sZ(s)+kb​Z(s)

    (m2​s2+cs+kb​)⋅X(s)=(cs+kb​)⋅Z(s)

    Z(s)=cs+kb​m2​s2+cs+kb​​X(s)

    Substituting Z(s) into the first differential equation,

    cs+kb​(m1​s2+cs+kt​+kb​)(m2​s2+cs+kb​)​X(s)=kt​Y(s)+(cs+kb​)⋅X(s)

    cs+kb​(m1​s2+cs+kt​+kb​)(m2​s2+cs+kb​)−(cs+kb​)2​X(s)=kt​Y(s)

    X(s)Y(s)​=(m1​s2+cs+kt​+kb​)(m2​s2+cs+kb​)−(cs+kb​)2kt​(cs+kb​)​

    #Question 2

    #Part (a)

    Assume x>y. Thus, the k2​ spring is in tension.

    Using Newton’s 2nd law on the mass,

    mx¨=f−k2​(x−y)

    mx¨=f−k2​x+k2​y

    Performing inverse Laplace transform,

    m⋅s2X(s)=F(s)−k2​X(s)+k2​Y(s)

    F(s)=(ms2+k2​)⋅X(s)−k2​Y(s)

    #Part (b)

    Since k2​ spring is in tension, k1​ spring will also be in tension.

    Using Newton’s 2nd law on the point between the springs,

    mx¨=k2​(x−y)−k1​(y)

    0=k2​x−k2​y−k1​y

    Performing inverse Laplace transform,

    0=k2​X(s)−k2​Y(s)−k1​Y(s)

    (k1​+k2​)⋅Y(s)=k2​X(s)

    Y(s)=k1​+k2​k2​​X(s)

    #Part (c)

    Substituting Y(s) into F(s),

    F(s)=(ms2+k2​)⋅X(s)−k2​Y(s)

    F(s)=(ms2+k2​)⋅X(s)−k1​+k2​(k2​)2​X(s)

    F(s)=[ms2+k2​−k1​+k2​(k2​)2​]X(s)

    F(s)=k1​+k2​(ms2+k2​)(k1​+k2​)−(k2​)2​X(s)

    F(s)X(s)​=(mk1​+mk2​)s2+k1​k2​k1​+k2​​

    #Part (d)

    Equivalent spring constant,

    keq​=1/k1​+1/k2​1​

    keq​=k1​+k2​k1​k2​​

    #Part (e)

    Substituting k1​=−1 into the transfer function,

    F(s)X(s)​=(mk2​−m)s2−k2​k2​−1​

    F(s)X(s)​=s2−k2​/(mk2​−m)(k2​−1)/(mk2​−m)​

    A=32​

    B=−32​

    C=1

    E=31​

    c(t)=32​e−2t−32​e−8t+1−34​e−2t+31​e−8t

    #Question 3

    A second-order system is described by the following differential equation:

    0.1dt2d2y​+0.2dtdy​+1.6y=1.6x

    Assume initial conditions are zeroes.

    (a) Use Laplace transform to determine the transfer function of the system.
    (b) Determine the undamped natural frequency and the damping ratio.
    (c) Determine the damped frequency.

    #Part (a)

    Performing Laplace transform,

    0.1s2Y(s)+0.2sY(s)+1.6Y(s)=1.6X(s)

    (0.1s2+0.2s+1.6)⋅Y(s)=1.6X(s)

    X(s)Y(s)​=0.1s2+0.2s+1.61.6​

    X(s)Y(s)​=s2+2s+1616​

    #Part (b)

    Comparing the transfer function with the general equation,

    X(s)Y(s)​=s2+2ζωn​s+ωn​2ωn​2​=s2+2s+1616​

    Undamped natural frequency,

    ωn​=16​=4 rad/s

    Damping ratio,

    2ζωn​=2

    2ζ(4)=2

    ζ=0.25

    #Part (c)

    Damped frequency,

    ωd​=ωn​1−ζ2​

    ωd​=41−0.252​

    ωd​=3.8730 rad/s

    #Question 4

    A feedback control system has characteristic equation: s3+6s2+13s+K=0.

    The parameter K must be positive. Using Routh-Hurwitz criterion, what is the
    maximum value of     K before the system becomes unstable? When K is equal
    to the maximum value, the system oscillates. Determine oscillation frequency,
    and the position of all the roots at that value of     K.

    #Maximum Value of K

    Applying the Routh-Hurwitz criterion,

    s3113
    s26K
    s1a1​=678−K​0
    s0b1​=K

    Workings for unknowns,

    a1​=66(13)−1(K)​=678−K​

    b1​=a1​a1​(K)−6(0)​=K

    From inspection of the 3rd row,

    678−K​>0

    K<78

    Range of values,

    0<K<78

    Thus, the maximum value of K is 78.

    #Oscillation Frequency

    Substituting K=78 into the Routh table,

    s3113
    s2678
    s100
    s00

    Since the 3rd row becomes a row of zeroes, we need to form
    an auxiliary equation using the coefficients from the 2nd row.

    Auxiliary equation,

    6s2+78   →   s2+13

    Oscillation frequency,

    0=s2+13

    s=±−13​

    s=±j13​

    ω=13​ rad/s

    #Position of Roots

    From the previous answer, two of the roots are,

    s1​=j13​

    s2​=−j13​

    To obtain the third root, divide characteristic equation by the auxiliary equation.

    s2+13s3+6s2+13s+78​=s+6

    s3​=−6

    #S1 (2025 - 2026)

    #Question 1

    A 2nd-order system is described by the differential equation,

    1.5y¨​+3.0y˙​+6.0y=6.0x

    where x is the input and y is the output of the system.

    Assume initial conditions are zeroes.

    (a) Using Laplace transform, determine the transfer function of the system.

    (b) Determine the undamped natural frequency (in rad/sec) and the damping ratio.

    (c) Determine the damped frequency (in rad/sec).

    (d) Determine MP​, tp​, and 2% ts​ of the response when subjected to a unit step input.

    Performing Laplace transform,

    L{1.5y¨​+3.0y˙​+6.0y}=L{6.0x}

    1.5s2⋅Y(s)+3.0s⋅Y(s)+6.0⋅Y(s)=6.0⋅X(s)

    (1.5s2+3.0s+6.0)⋅Y(s)=6.0⋅X(s)

    X(s)Y(s)​=1.5s2+3.0s+6.06.0​=s2+2s+44​

    Comparing with 2nd-order general equation,

    X(s)Y(s)​=s2+2ζωn​s+ωn​2ωn​​=s2+2s+44​

    Undamped natural frequency,

    ωn​=4​=2 rad/s

    Damping ratio,

    2ζωn​=2

    ζ=0.5

    Damped frequency,

    ωd​=ωn​1−ζ2​

    ωd​=21−0.52​

    ωd​=3​ rad/s

    Percent overshoot,

    MP​=e1−ζ2​−ζπ​=e1−0.52​−0.5π​

    MP​=0.16303

    Peak time,

    tr​=ωd​π​=3​π​

    tr​=1.8138 s

    2% settling time,

    ts(2%)​=ζωn​4​=0.5(2)4​

    ts(2%)​=4 s

    #Question 2

    The transfer function that relates the output response Y(s)
    to the input command     R(s) in a control system is given by,

    R(s)Y(s)​=s2+8s+1510(s+2)​

    (a) Determine y(t) of the system when it is subjected to a unit step input.

    (b) Determine the steady-state value of the system.

    Output response of system,

    R(s)Y(s)​=s2+8s+1510(s+2)​

    1/sY(s)​=(s+3)(s+5)10(s+2)​

    Y(s)=s(s+3)(s+5)10(s+2)​

    Y(s)=sA​+s+3B​+s+5C​

    Solving for partial fractions,

    10(s+2)=A(s+3)(s+5)+Bs(s+5)+Cs(s+3)

    Let s=0.

    10(2)=A(3)(5)

    A=34​

    Let s=−3.

    10(−1)=−3B(2)

    B=35​

    Let s=−5.

    10(−3)=−5C(−2)

    C=−3

    Output response of system,

    Y(s)=s4/3​+s+35/3​−s+53​

    Performing inverse Laplace transform,

    y(t)=34​+35​e−3t−3e−5t

    Steady-state value of system,

    t→∞lim​ y(t)=34​

    #CA2 S2 (2023 - 2024)

    #Question 1

    #Part (a)

    Transfer function of the system,

    R(s)C(s)​=InputOutput​=T(s)X(s)​

    Applying Newton’s 2nd law on the mass,

    mx¨=∑F

    mx¨=Fpinion​−(K1​x+Cx˙)−(f+K2​x)

    Fpinion​=mx¨+Cx˙+(K1​+K2​)x+f

    Applying Newton’s 2nd law on the pinion,

    Jθ¨=τ−Fpinion​r

    Fpinion​=rτ−Jθ¨​

    Fpinion​=rτ−J(x¨/r)​

    Fpinion​=rτ​−r2Jx¨​

    Substituting into the equation for the mass,

    rτ​−r2Jx¨​=mx¨+Cx˙+(K1​+K2​)x+f

    rτ​=(m+r2J​)x¨+Cx˙+(K1​+K2​)x+f

    Performing Laplace transform,

    rT(s)​=(m+r2J​)⋅s2X(s)+C⋅sX(s)+(K1​+K2​)⋅X(s)+sf​

    rT(s)​=X(s)⋅[(m+r2J​)s2+Cs+(K1​+K2​)]+sf​

    #Part (a)

    Between 100<ω<101, magnitude is flat (constant).
    Between 101<ω<102, magnitude increases at 20 db/dec (1st-order zero).
    Between 103<ω<104, magnitude decreases at −40 db/dec (2nd-order pole).

    Transfer function consists of:

    • Constant K
    • One 1st-order zero
    • One 1st-order pole
    • One 2nd-order pole

    Note the change in gradient from 20 db/dec to −40 db/dec.
    There must be a 1st-order pole to cancel out the 1st-order zero.
    Thus, the resulting gradient will be due to the 2nd-order pole.

    Value of constant,

    20lgK=20

    K=10

    Magnitude gradient begins to increase at 20 db/dec when ω≈30 rad/s.
    Thus, the expression for the 1st-order zero is approximated as as+a​=30s+30​.

    The spike in magnitude occurs at ω=200 rad/s. Let ζ=0.01.
    Thus, expression for 2nd-order pole is approximated as s2+4s+20022002​.

    Phase angle decreases at a rate of −4π​ rad/dec when ω≈1000 rad/s.
    Thus, expression for the 1st-order pole is approximated as s+aa​=s+10001000​.

    Transfer function of system,

    G(s)=10(30s+30​)(s+10001000​)(s2+4s+20022002​)

    Between 10−1<ω<101, magnitude decreases at −20 db/dec.
    Thus, the transfer function must contain an integrator s1​.

    Between 102<ω<103, magnitude decreases at −60 db/dec, which
    would indicate a further decrease by −40 db/dec from −20 db/dec.
    Thus, the transfer function must contain a 2nd-order pole.

    Between 103<ω<104, magnitude is relatively constant at −15 db,
    which would indicate an increase by +60 db/dec from −60 db/dec.
    Thus, transfer function must contain 1st-order and 2nd-order zeros.

    #EST S1 (2023 - 2024)

    #Part (a)

    Closed-loop transfer function,

    #Part (b)

    Applying Newton’s 2nd law,

    my¨​=b(u˙−y˙​)−ky

    my¨​=bu˙−by˙​−ky

    bu˙=my¨​+by˙​+ky

    2u˙=2y¨​+2y˙​+y

    Performing Laplace transform,

    b⋅sU(s)=m⋅s2Y(s)+b⋅sY(s)+k⋅Y(s)

    bs⋅U(s)=(ms2+bs+k)⋅Y(s)

    U(s)Y(s)​=ms2+bs+kbs​

    U(s)Y(s)​=2s2+2s+12s​

    #Part (c)

    Transfer function of system,

    θi​(s)θo​(s)​=s(Ts+1)+KK​

    θi​(s)θo​(s)​=Ts2+s+KK​

    θi​(s)θo​(s)​=s2+s/T+K/TK/T​

    Natural frequency of system,

    ωn​=TK​​

    Transfer function for 2nd-order system,

    InputOutput​=s2+2ζωn​s+ωn​2ωn​2​

    Damping ratio of system,

    T1​=2ζωn​

    T1​=2ζTK​​

    ζ=2T1​KT​​

    ζ2=4TK1​

    Peak time of response curve,

    tp​=ωd​π​=ωn​1−ζ2​π​

    ωn​1−ζ2​=tp​π​

    ωn​2(1−ζ2)=(tp​π​)2

    TK​(1−4TK1​)=9π2​

    TK​−4T21​=9π2​

    TK​=9π2​+4T21​

    K=9Tπ2​+4T1​

    Percent overshoot of response curve,

    Mp​=e−ζπ/1−ζ2​

    ln(Mp​)=−1−ζ2​ζπ​

    ln(Mp​)1−ζ2​=−ζπ

    [ln(Mp​)]2(1−ζ2)=ζ2π2

    [ln(Mp​)]2=ζ2(π2+[ln(Mp​)]2)

    ζ2=π2+[ln(Mp​)]2[ln(Mp​)]2​

    4TK1​=π2+(ln0.254)2(ln0.254)2​

    K=T1.5638​

    Equating the above equations,

    9Tπ2​+4T1​=T1.5638​

    91​π2T2+41​=1.5638

    T=1.0946

    K=1.4287

    #Part (b)

    1. Between 10−1<ω<100, magnitude is relatively flat
    2. Between 100<ω<101, magnitude increases at +20 db/dec
    3. Between 102<ω<103, magnitude decreases at −20 db/dec
    4. Sharp spike indicates a 2nd-order pole with very low damping ratio ζ

    Components of transfer function:

    • From observation 1, contains a constant K
    • From observation 2, contains a 1st-order zero
    • From observations 3 and 4, contains a 2nd-order pole

    Spike occurs at resonant frequency ωr​=40 rad/s.
    Assume a very low damping ratio of ζ=0.01.

    Natural frequency of system,

    ωr​=ωn​1−2ζ2​

    40=ωn​1−2(0.01)2​

    ωn​=40 rad/s

    Phase angle of 1st-order zero as+a​, where a=1, is ∠G(s)=2π​.

    Value of a is the point at which magnitude begins to increase.

    Phase angle of 2nd-order pole s2+2ζωn​s+ωn​2ωn​2​, where ωn​=40, is ∠G(s)=−π.

    Value of ωn​ is obtained from the resonant frequency equation.

    #Part (c)

    Unity feedback system is a Type 0 system.

    Steady-state error (unit step input),

    ess​=1+Kp​1​

    The static position error constant is obtained
    from the magnitude at the lowest value of ω.

    From the magnitude plot,

    −4=20lgKp​

    Kp​=0.63096

    Steady-state error (unit step input),

    ess​=1+0.630961​=0.61314

    Steady-state error (unit ramp input),

    ess​=∞

    Note that unit ramp input is Type 1 input. Since input is of a
    higher type than the system, the steady-state error is infinity.
